L14@P0: Abstract: Since the evolution of the electric and hybrid vehicle, the analysis of batteries’ characteristics
L15@P0: and influence on driving range has become essential. This fact advocates the necessity of accurate
L16@P0: simulation modeling for batteries. Different models for the Li-ion battery cell are reviewed in this
L17@P0: paper and a group of the highly dynamic models is selected for comparison. A new open circuit
L18@P0: voltage (OCV) model is proposed. The new model can simulate the OCV curves of lithium iron
L19@P0: magnesium phosphate (LiFeMgPO4) battery type at different temperatures. It also considers both
L20@P0: charging and discharging cases. The most remarkable features from different models, in addition
L21@P0: to the proposed OCV model, are integrated in a single hybrid electrical model. A lumped thermal
L22@P0: model is implemented to simulate the temperature development in the battery cell. The synthesized
L23@P0: electro-thermal battery cell model is extended to model a battery pack of an actual electric vehicle.
L24@P0: Experimental tests on the battery, as well as drive tests on the vehicle are performed. The proposed
L25@P0: model demonstrates a higher modeling accuracy, for the battery pack voltage, than the constituent
L26@P0: models under extreme maneuver drive tests.
L27@P0: Keywords: temperature influence; new OCV model; battery circuit model; synthesized battery model;
L28@P0: thermal model; electric vehicle
L29@P0: 1. Introduction
L30@P0: The global climate change, escalation in fuel cost, and the energy consumption, urged the necessity
L31@P0: to replace the fossil fuel with renewable and environment friendly energy sources. Battery electric
L32@P0: vehicles (BEV) are one major application, demonstrating the replacement of fossil fuel by renewable
L33@P0: energy. Li-ion batteries have become the preferable energy storage for the future electric vehicles [1].
L34@P0: They receive greater attention than other battery types, such as lead-acid and nickel-cadmium batteries,
L35@P0: due to their practical physical characteristics. They have a high specific energy, specific power, power
L36@P0: density and a long life cycle. Moreover, their self-discharge rate is lower compared to other types of
L37@P0: batteries [1–3].
L38@P0: Figure 1 demonstrates a typical discharge characteristic curve of a lithium-ion battery. The battery
L39@P0: voltage extends between an upper and lower voltage limits Vfull and Vcut-off, respectively. Vcut-off
L40@P0: represents the empty state of the battery where the minimum allowable voltage is reached.
L41@P0: This restriction is meant to protect the battery from deep depletion. The section formed between Vfull,
L42@P0: Vexp and the correspondences capacity rates (C-rate) 0 and Qexp is identified as the exponential region
L43@P0: of the discharge characteristic curve, at which the discharged voltage changes exponentially regarding
L44@P0: to the battery capacity. The voltage holds an approximately steady value for C-rates beyond Qexp up to
L45@P0: the nominal C-rate Qnom, where the nominal Vnom voltage is reached. Not only is the battery voltage

L55@P1: The vehicle under test (VUT) is equipped with battery cells of a cathode type LiFeMgPO4.
L56@P1: Lithium iron phosphate cells are characterized by their flat open circuit voltage curve (OCV). Hence,
L57@P1: the cell voltage stays almost constant over the complete state of charge (SOC) range [2,3,6]. The
L58@P1: battery pack of the VUT consists of 19 modules. Each module comprises six cell blocks connected in
L59@P1: series; a single cell block is constructed out of 50 LiFeMgPO4–graphite cells, connected in parallel. In
L60@P1: total, there are 300 cells within the single battery module. Each cell block has a nominal voltage of 3.2
L61@P1: V, amounting to a total voltage of 19.2 V. The battery specifications are given in Table 1. A Controller
L62@P1: Area Network (CAN) communication environment is used for the control and management of the
L63@P1: battery modules. More technical information about the VUT is available in the Appendix.

L270: #### cite146†Description L271: ## Product Description
L272: 
L273: This Low-Light HD USB Camera is ideally suited to use underwater with excellent low-light performance, good color handling, and onboard video compression. A specially-chosen wide-angle, low distortion lens provides excellent picture quality on the ROV, and a built-in microphone* allows listening to sounds of the deep, and your vehicle.
L274: Based on the Sony IMX322/323 sensor, this camera uses a large sensor (1/2.9″) and a relatively low pixel count (2MP, 1080p), meaning that the physical pixel size is large to allow maximum light sensitivity. We’ve had this camera down at 300m depth, where we could see subtle bioluminescent creatures in the darkness!
L275: The camera also has an onboard H.264 compression chip so that all of the video compression is done onboard and doesn’t place much load on the main computer. That also means that we’ll be able to support multiple cameras in the future for alternate views.
L276: 
L277: This camera is fully supported in ArduSub. Includes an 8″ USB cable with JST-PH connector.
L278: 
L279: The camera’s PCB is 32 x 32mm and works well with our cite147†Camera Tilt System .
